paragraphs.text: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia type 3 (FHH3) is an autosomal dominant disorder of extracellular calcium homeostasis that affects the parathyroids, kidneys, and bone. Like the other types of FHH, it is marked by lifelong high serum calcium with inappropriately low urinary calcium excretion. Nesbit et al. (2013) noted that FHH3 also has distinctive features: increased serum parathyroid hormone (PTH), hypophosphatemia, and osteomalacia. Howles et al. (2016) described type 3 as the most clinically severe variant of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia.

paragraphs.text: McMurtry et al. (1992) studied a large kindred with familial benign hypercalcemia. After the proposita was identified, 46 kindred members from 5 generations, aged 1.5 to 91 years, were surveyed biochemically and/or by chart review, and 19 were affected. In 15 hypercalcemic subjects examined biochemically, serum immunoreactive PTH, measured in 3 separate immunoassays, became supranormal by about age 30 years and appeared to rise further after that. These subjects had normal serum alkaline phosphatase activity and creatinine, but their inorganic phosphate levels were lower than those of unaffected kindred members. Of 5 affected adults older than 40 years who were studied radiographically, 3 had changes suggestive of osteomalacia. In one of them, a 51-year-old woman, iliac crest biopsy after tetracycline labeling confirmed defective skeletal mineralization. McMurtry et al. (1992) concluded that in this kindred the disorder could be especially hard to distinguish from primary hyperparathyroidism in adults, and that it might not be entirely benign, because osteomalacia, perhaps due to mild hypophosphatemia, could develop in adulthood.

paragraphs.text: Hannan et al. (2010) studied 24 polymorphic loci in the Oklahoma kindred and found a peak LOD score of 6.92 at 0% recombination with D19S606. Recombinants in 3 individuals narrowed the FBHH3 locus to a 4.1-Mb region flanked centromerically by D19S112 and telomerically by rs245111. The syntenic region on mouse chromosome 7 contains 4 Casr-related sequences (Gprc2a-rs), but no human homologs were found. Comparison of the 22.0-Mb human region with the 39.3-Mb mouse region showed 2 evolutionarily conserved segments that were inverted in humans, and an 11.6-Mb mouse segment containing the 4 Gprc2a-rs genes was absent from the human genome. The authors also sequenced the coding regions and intron-exon boundaries of 12 other genes in the interval that are expressed in the parathyroids and/or kidneys, in an affected individual. They found no abnormalities, and RT-PCR excluded splicing defects.

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on one affected individual from each of 2 unrelated FHH3 kindreds: the Oklahoma kindred and the FHH3NI kindred. Within the 3.46-Mbp FHH3 interval on 19q13.3, both patients carried the same C-to-T transition in exon 2 of the AP2S1 gene, predicting an arg15-to-cys (R15C) substitution. Dideoxynucleotide sequencing confirmed the change. Restriction enzyme analysis showed that it cosegregated with the disorder in 32 affected and 23 unaffected members from 4 generations of the 2 kindreds. The authors then sequenced AP2S1 in 50 unrelated FHH patients without CASR mutations. They found 11 heterozygous missense mutations, all affecting arg15: 4 R15C, 3 arg15-to-his (R15H), and 4 arg15-to-leu (R15L). Based on this, they estimated that arg15 AP2S1 mutations may cause FHH in more than 20% of patients without CASR mutations. Arg15 is conserved in all AP2-sigma-2 orthologs and in all human AP sigma paralogs. In the crystal structure of AP2, it forms key contacts with dileucine-based motifs of cargo proteins. Functional studies in HEK293 cells that stably expressed CASR gave 3 main results: - Expression of each of the 3 mutant proteins shifted the concentration-response curves to the right and significantly raised the EC50, indicating that the cells were less sensitive to extracellular calcium. - The R15C mutant reduced CASR endocytosis compared with wildtype. - Mutating the C-terminal dileucine motif of CASR also reduced the receptor's sensitivity to extracellular calcium.
